title: [Residence for Marshall and Nannie S. Field, 1905 South Prairie Avenue, Chicago, Illinois]. [First floor plan].
creator: Hunt, Richard Morris, 1827-1895 (architect)
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
collection: The Hunt Collection in the AIA/AAF Collection (Library of Congress)
rights_basis: LoC: No known restrictions on publication.
notes: Hunt office drawing ('No. 2, office copy'; inscribed 'M. Field' and 'Plan of Principal Floor'; 'This drawing to be returned to R. M. Hunt Archt.'), ink and wash with red-tinted masonry walls and a scale bar. Shows the principal-floor plan of the Field house: canted/octagonal-cornered rooms, a large circular stair hall projecting at the top of the sheet, a curved bay (hatched) on one side, and the entrance steps at the bottom of the sheet (the street front; the house stood on the east side of Prairie, facing west). The only Hunt drawing for the Field house LoC has digitized (searches 'Marshall and Nannie S. Field', 'Hunt Field residence Chicago', 'Richard Morris Hunt Chicago' all return only this plan). A design-stage drawing: as-built and any 1873–1904 changes need confirming against the 1886/1911 Sanborn footprints. Published as fig. 3.16b in Sam Watters, The Gilded Life of Richard Morris Hunt (2024). Scale bar on sheet — footprint dimensions could be measured from the TIFF (master: tile.loc.gov/storage-services/master/pnp/ppmsca/58300/58353u.tif).

title: [Residence of Marshall and Nannie S. Field, 1905 South Prairie Avenue, Chicago, Illinois. Entrance hall].
creator: unknown photographer (published in George W. Sheldon, Artistic Houses)
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
call_number: Illus. in NA7207.A72, v.2, pt. 1 [P&P]; LC-DIG-ppmsca-56274
rights_basis: LoC: No known restrictions on publication.
notes: Entrance hall with fireplace, staircase and furnishings; decorator L. Marcotte & Co.; Hunt design 1871–73. LoC note says published in Sheldon, Artistic Houses vol. 1 pt. 2 (1883) though the call number cites v.2 pt.1; also fig. 3.16a in Watters 2024. Interior state c. 1880; Field lived here until his death in 1906, so the hall in 1904 was likely similar but redecoration between 1880 and 1904 is unverified. No exterior information.

repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division

title: 2.  Historic American Buildings Survey Albert J. DeLong, Photographer April 3, 1935 NORTH AND EAST ELEVATIONS - Henry Clarke House, 4526 South Wabash Avenue (moved from Michigan Avenue), Chicago, Cook County, IL
camera_position: from the street at 4526 S. Wabash Avenue
creator: Albert J. DeLong (HABS photographer)
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
rights_basis: No known restrictions on images made by the U.S. Government; images copied from other sources may be restricted (LoC HABS rights statement)
notes: The Clarke house at its 1904 site, 4526 S. Wabash Avenue (north and east elevations), photographed 1935 — the closest documented view of how it looked in 1904 (it stood here 1872–1977). Shows the two-storey clapboard frame block with central pediment gable, square cupola, end chimneys, no portico (removed at the 1872 move), high basement and exterior stoops; a brick apartment building crowds the lot. Not on Prairie Avenue in 1904; record exists as the anachronism guard for the modern 1827 S. Indiana site.

title: 1. Title Sheet - Second Presbyterian Church, 1936 South Michigan Avenue, Chicago, Cook County, IL
creator: Hagerty, Duane (delineator), School of the Art Institute of Chicago Historic Preservation Program, for HABS (2011 Peterson Prize entry)
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
rights_basis: No known restrictions on images made by the U.S. Government; images copied from other sources may be restricted (LoC HABS rights statement)
notes: HABS measured drawing (2010): title sheet with history text and a drawing of a triple art-glass window. Records the building as surveyed in 2010. For 1904: the Joliet-limestone Renwick shell (1872–74) and tower survive from before 1904, and the interior is the post-1900-fire Howard Van Doren Shaw / Frederic Clay Bartlett rebuild (the 1900 fire destroyed the sanctuary roof — HABS data p.1), so the drawn roof structure and interior reflect c. 1900–01 work that was in place by 1904; later changes (1904–2010) are not itemized in the HABS report and need checking (e.g. any loss of tower/spire elements). Dimension datums on the sheet; full-resolution master TIFF at …/il0992/sheet/00001a.tif.

creator: Stephanie Gawur and Emily Wallrath, SAIC Historic Preservation Program, for HABS

rights_basis: No known restrictions on images made by the U.S. Government; images copied from other sources may be restricted (LoC HABS rights statement)
notes: 3-page HABS report (read in full). Exterior: Gothic Revival, cream-coloured, tar-stained rusticated Joliet limestone on south and east facades, common brick on north and west; prominent bell tower at SE corner; pointed-arch windows N and S; non-traditional two-aisle plan. History: Renwick building completed 1874; 1900 fire completely destroyed the sanctuary roof and smoke/water-damaged the nave; Howard Van Doren Shaw (a member) redesigned the interior in Arts and Crafts style (altered arches, supports and ceilings; art glass; murals; 175 angels; electrified fixtures); Frederic Clay Bartlett tree-of-life mural behind the choir loft. Coordinates 41.855696 N, -87.624367 W. NRHP 74000754. No numeric dimensions in the text (the 22 sheets carry them).
